learn: Artists use many kinds of lines: straight, curved, zigzag, spiral, dotted, broken, thick and thin.
Changing how hard you press makes lines thick or thin.
A drawing with many kinds of lines looks lively.
check: How can you make a line thicker?
Which is a kind of line?
Many kinds of lines make a drawing look...
lessons.try: Fill a page with ten different kinds of lines.

learn: Lines are all around us: tree branches, cracks in the sidewalk, power wires, stripes on a shirt.
Horizontal lines go side to side, like the horizon. Vertical lines go up and down, like a flagpole.
Diagonal lines slant and can make a picture feel like it's moving.
check: Diagonal lines can make a picture feel...
lessons.try: Go on a line hunt and find five horizontal, vertical and diagonal lines.

learn: A line drawing uses only lines, with no colour or shading.
Artists use line to show shapes, details and texture.
Try a blind contour: draw an object while looking only at it, not your paper. It's fun and builds careful looking.
check: In a blind contour, you look at...
lessons.try: Do a blind contour drawing of your shoe.

learn: A shape is a flat area with length and width.
Geometric shapes have exact edges. Organic shapes are free-form, like puddles.
Positive shapes are the objects. Negative space is the empty space around them.
check: The empty space around objects is...
lessons.try: Cut a shape from paper. Look at both the shape and the hole it left.

learn: A form has length, width and depth. You can walk around it.
Spheres, cubes, cylinders, cones and pyramids are geometric forms.
Your body, a tree and a cloud are organic forms.
check: A form has length, width and...
An ice cream cone is shaped like a...
lessons.try: Find one example of each geometric form at home.

lessons.t: Drawing Shapes to Look Like Forms
learn: Shading makes a flat shape look 3D.
Light hits one side of a ball. The other side is darker.
Shade gradually from light to dark to show roundness.
check: What makes a flat shape look 3D?
The side away from the light is...
lessons.try: Draw a circle, then shade it to look like a ball.

learn: Primary colours are red, yellow and blue.
Secondary colours are orange, green and purple, made by mixing two primaries.
Tertiary colours are made by mixing a primary and a secondary next to it: red-orange, yellow-green, blue-purple.
check: How many primary colours are there?
Mixing a primary and a secondary next to it makes a...
lessons.try: Mix yellow and green to make yellow-green.

learn: The full wheel has 12 colours: 3 primary, 3 secondary and 6 tertiary.
Colours next to each other are analogous and look calm together.
Colours across from each other are complementary and look bold together.
check: How many colours on the full wheel?
Colours next to each other are...
Colours across from each other are...
lessons.try: Paint a 12-colour wheel.

learn: A tint is a colour plus white. Pink is a tint of red.
A shade is a colour plus black. Navy is a shade of blue.
Artists use tints and shades to show light and shadow.
check: A tint is a colour plus...
A shade is a colour plus...
lessons.try: Make three tints and three shades of one colour.

learn: Warm colours are red, orange and yellow. They seem to come forward in a picture.
Cool colours are blue, green and purple. They seem to go back.
This helps artists show near and far.
lessons.try: Paint mountains far away in cool colours and a field up close in warm colours.

learn: Warm colours can feel happy, energetic or angry.
Cool colours can feel calm, peaceful or sad.
Artists choose colours to share feelings.
check: Why do artists choose certain colours?
lessons.try: Make two drawings of the same face: one in warm colours and one in cool. How does each feel?

learn: Vincent van Gogh painted "The Starry Night" in 1889 with swirling blue sky and yellow stars.
The cool blues feel like night. The warm yellows glow like light.
Mixing warm and cool makes the picture exciting.
check: In that painting, the stars are...
Mixing warm and cool colours makes a picture...
lessons.try: Paint a night sky with cool blues and warm yellow stars.

learn: Actual texture can be felt, like tree bark or a wool scarf.
Implied texture is drawn to look like a texture, but is smooth to the touch.
Artists use lines and dots to imply texture.
lessons.try: Draw the texture of a pinecone without touching paper to cone.

learn: Hatching uses lines side by side. Cross-hatching crosses them.
Stippling uses many dots. Close dots look darker.
These marks make texture and shadow.
lessons.try: Shade three squares: hatching, cross-hatching and stippling.

learn: Mixed media means using more than one material in one artwork.
You can add fabric, sand, yarn or crumpled paper for real texture.
Glue thick materials first and let them dry.
check: What should you do after gluing thick materials?
lessons.try: Make a mixed media landscape with at least three textures.

learn: A motif is the shape or picture that repeats in a pattern.
A motif can be simple, like a star, or detailed, like a flower.
Wallpaper and fabric often repeat a motif.
check: The shape that repeats in a pattern
lessons.try: Design a motif and repeat it across a page.

learn: An alternating pattern switches between two or more motifs: star, moon, star, moon.
A rotating pattern turns the motif each time.
Changing colour, size or direction makes patterns interesting.
lessons.try: Make a rotating pattern with a triangle.

learn: Nature makes patterns: zebra stripes, honeycombs, sunflower seeds and snail shells.
Many cultures use patterns in weaving, pottery and buildings.
Islamic art often uses beautiful geometric tile patterns.
check: Which is a pattern in nature?
lessons.try: Find a pattern in nature and sketch it.

learn: Observation drawing means drawing what you really see, not what you think something looks like.
Look more than you draw: look, draw a little, look again.
Start with big shapes, then add details.
lessons.try: Draw a fruit while looking at it closely.

learn: A still life is a drawing or painting of objects that don't move, like fruit, bottles and flowers.
Artists arrange objects so some overlap and some are in front.
Light from one side makes clear shadows.
check: Art of objects that don't move
lessons.try: Arrange three objects and draw a still life.

learn: A portrait shows a person. A self-portrait shows the artist.
Eyes are halfway down the head. The bottom of the nose is halfway between eyes and chin.
Look at the shapes of features: almond eyes, a triangle nose, curved lips.
check: Where are the eyes on a head?
lessons.try: Draw a portrait of a family member.

learn: In a relief print, the raised parts get ink and print. The cut-away parts stay paper colour.
Stamps, foam plates and woodcuts are relief prints.
The image prints in reverse, like in a mirror.
check: In a relief print, what gets ink?
lessons.try: Make a foam plate print of a simple animal.

learn: A monoprint makes only one print.
Paint on a smooth tray, press paper on it, and peel.
Each monoprint is unique.
check: How many prints does a monoprint make?
Where do you paint for a monoprint?
lessons.try: Paint on a tray and pull a monoprint.

learn: An edition is a set of matching prints from one plate.
Artists number them: 1/5 means the first of five.
Clean edges and even ink make a good edition.
lessons.try: Make three matching prints and number them.

learn: Additive sculpture builds up by adding materials, like clay or recycled boxes.
Subtractive sculpture takes material away, like carving soap or wood.
Carving tools must be used carefully, with a grown-up's help.
check: Who should help with carving tools?
lessons.try: Carve a simple shape from a bar of soap with a plastic knife and a grown-up.

learn: A relief sculpture sticks out from a flat background, like the faces on coins.
A free-standing sculpture can be seen from all sides.
Both use form and texture.
check: A free-standing sculpture can be seen...
lessons.try: Make a relief sculpture by pressing shapes into clay.

learn: Architecture is the art of designing buildings.
Architects plan how a building looks and how people use it.
Famous buildings include the Taj Mahal in India and the pyramids of Egypt.
check: How a building looks and is used
lessons.try: Design and build a model house from paper and tape.

learn: Ancient Egyptian artists painted on tomb walls and carved huge statues.
They drew people with heads and legs from the side and bodies from the front.
They wrote with picture symbols called hieroglyphs.
check: What were Egyptian picture symbols called?
Egyptian artists drew heads from the...
lessons.try: Write your name with made-up picture symbols, like hieroglyphs.

learn: Aboriginal Australian artists use dot painting to tell stories about the land.
Chinese artists paint with ink and brush on silk or paper, often showing mountains and bamboo.
Native American artists create beadwork, pottery and weaving with special meanings.
check: Who uses dot painting to tell stories?
lessons.try: Make a dot painting with cotton swabs.

learn: Art from other cultures can teach us how people live and what they believe.
When we learn about it, we use the right names and say where it comes from.
We can be inspired by other art without copying sacred designs.
check: What can art from other cultures teach us?
When we learn about it, we...
No, we can be inspired instead
lessons.try: Find one fact about an artwork from another culture and share it.
